passage: The B.Sc. results were pasted outside the college office in Sagar. Tanuja found her name: a pass in chemistry, but lower than she'd hoped. Zeenat, beside her, was fuming. "That paper was unfair. Everyone says it was the toughest in years." Tanuja nodded slowly. "It was tough. That wasn't in my hands." She thought about the organic unit she'd skimmed because it bored her, and the three questions from it she'd left blank. "But I also skipped organic. That part was mine." On the bus home, past the mustard fields, she wrote in her notebook: "Next sem: organic first, practice papers from the last five years. Tough papers will happen." She felt steadier than she had that morning.

qa.q: What did Tanuja write in her notebook on the bus?
qa.a: "Next sem: organic first, practice papers from the last five years. Tough papers will happen."

qa.q: Why did Tanuja feel steadier by the end of the day?
qa.a: Seeing both the tough paper and the skipped unit let her avoid both blaming others and blaming only herself, and gave her a plan she could act on.

qa.q: Which choice showed a balanced response to the result?
qa.a: Accepting the paper's difficulty as outside her control while owning the skipped organic unit, then planning practice papers.

qa.q: How might Zeenat see the same result differently?
qa.a: Zeenat sees only the unfair paper, which may protect her from disappointment but gives her nothing to change for next time.

passage: At the welcome dinner in Edinburgh, Felix asked Mei how she'd won the scholarship. She started to say "hard work", then stopped. It was true: two years of late nights over maths. But she also thought of her school in Singapore, the well-stocked lab, the teacher who stayed after class, her parents who could afford books. "Honestly? A lot of work and a lot of luck." Felix laughed. "At least you admit the luck." Mei smiled, but that night she made a list. She couldn't choose where she'd grown up. She could choose to go to office hours every week, to volunteer with the tutoring scheme for first-generation students, and to keep up the late nights when they mattered.

qa.q: What was Mei's honest answer to Felix?
qa.a: "A lot of work and a lot of luck."

qa.q: Why did Mei stop before saying only "hard work"?
qa.a: Mei felt uneasy taking all the credit, because she recognised the school, teacher and books she was lucky to have, alongside her own effort.

qa.q: What choices did Mei list, and why do they fit a balanced view?
qa.a: Weekly office hours, volunteering with the tutoring scheme and keeping up the late nights; they act on what she controls without pretending luck played no part.

qa.q: Why might Felix appreciate Mei admitting the luck?
qa.a: Felix may not have had the same advantages, so hearing Mei name them feels honest and respectful of different starting points.

grounding: A student acknowledges both effort and privilege in her scholarship and chooses actions she can control.

qa.a: Splitting the result into luck and his own share frees him from blaming fate or himself entirely, which feels lighter and more hopeful.

qa.a: Admitting the unlucky graph question while owning the fumbled array questions, then planning practice and mock interviews.

passage:
Dear Jomon,
You asked how I feel about not getting into the architecture college in Thiruvananthapuram. Honestly, both things are true. I didn't practise enough freehand drawing; I know that. I spent too long on maths I already knew. But I also got the year when the paper had three perspective questions instead of one, and my exam centre had a power cut for twenty minutes. That was luck, and it wasn't mine.
So I'm not calling myself stupid, and I'm not blaming the universe. I've joined a weekend drawing class, and I'm making a timetable that puts drawing first. If the paper's cruel again next year, fine. At least the drawing part will be mine.
Your sister,
Seema

grounding: A student sees that both her own preparation and bad luck shaped an admission result, and acts on the part she can change.

passage: Himani, you keep saying I'm lucky I got into the Delhi college. Okay, let me be honest. Yes, I was lucky. My school had a proper library and a teacher who stayed after class for us. qa.q: What does Sarita focus on this semester, and why is that wise?
qa.a: Attendance, notes and sleep, the parts within reach; acting on those while letting go of the rest avoids both blame and helplessness.
